name: Hassan Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Hassan, 27, and I'm an assistant buyer at Brightwire Supplies, an electrical wholesaler. We sell cable, sockets, fuse boards and lighting to electricians and building firms. I live with my girlfriend Priya, who teaches at a primary school. I did my exams at school, went straight into the trade counter at 18, and I've been in purchasing for about a year and a half.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I check the stock report and see what's running low, like 2.5 mm twin and earth cable, which we go through like water. Then I raise orders with about thirty suppliers, chase late deliveries and ask for better prices, which I'm still not great at. My boss Martin signs off anything big. I like it when I get a good deal and the lads on the trade counter notice. What wears me out is copper prices, which jump around and wreck my quotes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool, not a takeover. I use one now and then to tidy up emails to suppliers when I'm annoyed and need to sound polite. I'd probably joke at the counter that the robots aren't coming for anyone's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be relieved, because I'm still learning and I'd like the time to get good. My boss Martin keeps saying it takes five years to become a proper buyer, and in this world I get those five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and ask Martin for more responsibility, maybe the lighting range on my own. Priya and I are saving for a flat deposit and we're about two thirds there, so I'd keep that going. I might use the email tool a bit more, but nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, like the plan still works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said copper prices wear you out. Does that stay the same here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Copper, always copper. When the price jumped last winter, a contractor cancelled an order for a whole housing site and Martin wasn't pleased with my quote. That's the real stress, and it would carry on exactly the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to be in a couple of years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Two years more, then the deposit, then a flat near Priya's school. I'd still want to be the person electricians ask for by name.

say: I'd say AI is a **tool, not a takeover**, good for tidying supplier emails.
I'd joke on the **trade counter** that the robots aren't coming for anyone.
think: I'd be **relieved** to get the five years Martin says it takes to learn buying.
My biggest stress stays **copper prices**, not software.
do: Ask Martin for the **lighting range** to run on my own.
Keep saving with Priya; the **flat deposit** is two thirds there.
feel: **Calm** and **settled**, because the plan still works.
S0.quote: My boss Martin keeps saying it takes five years to become a proper buyer, and in this world I get those five years.
fieldNote: His worries are about **copper prices** and quotes, the normal stress of the trade.
He uses AI lightly and treats it as **a tool**, not a threat.
The **flat deposit** with Priya is his main goal, and nothing here threatens it.

steps.text: Ask Martin to hand over the lighting range
Keep saving for the flat deposit with Priya

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say workers need a say in how this gets brought in, not just the bosses. I'd share stuff about unions in tech and retail, and I'd tell my mates that buying is exactly the kind of job they mean. People think wholesale is all forklifts, but it's mostly screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's on the list on that card. Buying, checking, planning: that's my whole day. The senior buyers know the suppliers personally, but I'm the one who mostly just raises orders, and software can do that already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd get properly good at the AI ordering tools before Brightwire forces them on us, so I'm the one who can run them. I'd also look at an electrician apprenticeship, because I know the kit and the electricians already. Priya and I would hold off on the flat for six months to see how it shakes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A knot in my stomach, but not total panic, because I've got options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on the flat. How would that conversation with Priya go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would hurt to pause, because we're so close. But I don't want a mortgage the year my job shrinks. Priya's job is steady, but a teacher's pay alone won't cover what we were planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gemma on the trade counter, actually, and Martin's assistant, Rob. Rob's been doing the same order checking for fifteen years. I can switch, but I'm not sure Rob can.

say: I'd say **workers need a say** in how AI comes in, not only bosses.
I'd tell mates that wholesale buying is **mostly screens**, exactly the work AI takes.
think: Buying, checking and planning are my **whole day**, so my job's on the list.
As the junior who mostly **raises orders**, I'm easy for software to replace.
do: Learn the **AI ordering tools** before Brightwire forces them on everyone.
Look into an **electrician apprenticeship**, using what I know about the kit.
Pause the **flat purchase** with Priya for six months.
feel: **Anxious**, a knot in the stomach, but not panic because there are **options**.
S1.quote: People think wholesale is all forklifts, but it's mostly screens.
fieldNote: He sees his day as **thinking work** and expects his role to shrink.
He hedges two ways: **learning tools** and a **trade switch**.
He worries for **older colleagues** like Rob more than himself.

steps.text: Learn Brightwire's new AI ordering system before it's rolled out
Ask a contractor customer about electrician apprenticeship places
Pause the flat purchase with Priya for six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to step in now, with wage support, maybe a basic income. I'd be signing every petition and I'd vote for whoever takes it seriously. Online I'd be the angry one, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my buying job's done by 2028. If AI can do any thinking work, it can raise orders and haggle with suppliers better than me. The hands-on side lasts till about 2031, so the electricians we supply have three more years than I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an electrician apprenticeship straight away, this year, even on lower pay. I'd use our deposit savings to cover the pay cut, which hurts. I'd want to qualify before 2028 if I could, but it's normally four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Like I'm running for a bus that's already pulling away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the apprenticeship takes four years and robots come by 2031, does the plan work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's the problem. I'd be half trained when the robots arrive in 2031. So maybe I'm buying three years at best. I'd still do it, because three years of work beats none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Priya say to each other that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk about it at the kitchen table, Priya would be calm, she always is. She'd say we can live on hers for a bit. But teachers might get hit too, with AI tutors, so I don't know if hers is safe either.

say: I'd say government must act now with **wage support** or a **basic income**.
I'd sign every petition and vote for whoever treats it **seriously**.
think: My buying job is **done by 2028**, because AGI can haggle better than me.
Electricians we supply get **three more years** than I do, until robots around 2031.
do: Start an **electrician apprenticeship** this year, even on lower pay.
Use the **deposit savings** to cover the pay cut while training.
feel: **Scared**, like running for a bus that's already pulling away.
S2.quote: The electricians we supply have three more years than I do.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** quickly and grabs the hands-on route anyway.
He sees the plan only buys **three years**, and goes ahead regardless.
He's unsure even **Priya's teaching job** is safe, which removes the household's anchor.
He puts his hope in **politics**: wage support and a basic income.

steps.text: Start an electrician apprenticeship this year on trainee pay
Spend part of the flat deposit to cover the pay cut
Vote for candidates promising a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough that nobody should be caught out, so unions and government need a plan now. I'd go to a union meeting for the first time, honestly. Brightwire isn't unionised but the warehouse lads talk about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job goes around 2031, but five years changes how I go about it. I can finish an apprenticeship properly. And I'd be qualified before the robots, so I'd get a few good years on the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrician apprenticeship next year, part time if Brightwire would let me. I'd keep enough of our savings for the deposit, and Priya and I would buy a smaller flat. I'd also get decent at the AI tools at work, so I'm useful till I leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but less frightened than the two-year one. Like I can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think being an electrician is safe for good?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. Robots do come in 2034, and by then I'd be 35. But I'd have a trade, savings, and a flat, and that's a better place to start again from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy the flat in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd buy it. A smaller one, near Priya's school, so she can walk. A home is the one thing I'd want sorted before it all changes.

say: I'd say five years is enough that **nobody** should be caught out.
I'd go to my first **union meeting**, even though Brightwire isn't unionised.
think: My buying job goes around **2031**, but five years lets me plan.
I can finish an apprenticeship and get a few years **on the tools** before robots.
do: Start a **part-time apprenticeship** next year if Brightwire allows it.
Buy a **smaller flat** near Priya's school, keeping part of the savings back.
Get decent at the **AI tools** at work so I'm useful until leaving.
feel: **Nervous** but less frightened, like being able to **see the road**.
S3.quote: A home is the one thing I'd want sorted before it all changes.
fieldNote: He still expects to lose the buying job, but the **warning time** gives him control.
He mixes **retraining**, using the tools at work, and securing a **home**.
He's honest that an electrician's trade isn't **safe for good** either.

steps.text: Start a part-time electrician apprenticeship next year
Buy a smaller flat near Priya's school
Use Brightwire's AI ordering tools until leaving
Attend a union meeting with the warehouse staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's use it to make it fair: retraining, shorter weeks, shared gains. I'd probably get involved in politics locally for the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine, probably. I'd be 37 in 2036, an electrician by then, and robots don't reach the tools till 2039. I'd still lose the buying job, but on my own timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep buying for two or three more years and learn as much as I can. Then I'd start the apprenticeship around 2029. Priya and I would buy the flat next year as planned and maybe think about kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. There's time, and that changes everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything make you rush, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, not with ten years. Most of my mates would have time too. It's more about the older lads at Brightwire, who'd be near retirement without much to show for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your rule for yourself, picturing this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use the slow years well. Get the deposit, get the trade, and keep an eye on the news so I don't get lazy about it.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift to use for fair retraining and **shared gains**.
I'd get involved in **local politics** for the first time.
think: I'd lose the buying job, but **on my own timing**.
By 2036 I'd be an electrician, with robots not reaching tools till **2039**.
do: Keep buying for two or three years and **learn** as much as possible.
Buy the **flat** with Priya next year as planned.
S4.quote: I'd still lose the buying job, but on my own timing.
fieldNote: He expects to leave buying but feels his **income is safe** through a planned trade switch.
Ten years turns fear into a **schedule**: deposit, apprenticeship, then children.
His concern shifts to **older colleagues** near retirement.

steps.text: Buy the flat with Priya next year
Join the local party branch pushing retraining funds

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's the only one where I can't get a trade in time and even Priya's job might wobble. What would help is paid apprenticeships for adults, so you don't have to burn your savings to retrain, and some kind of wage support while you do it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who I'd blame. I wouldn't blame AI itself, I'd blame the people deciding to keep all the savings for themselves. If the gains were shared, I'd be much less worried.

headlineQuote: I wouldn't blame AI itself, I'd blame the people deciding to keep all the savings for themselves.
portrait: Hassan is a **27-year-old** assistant buyer at Brightwire, an electrical wholesaler.
He lives with Priya, a teacher, and they're saving for a **flat deposit**.
He uses AI now and then and sees his own day as **mostly screen work**.
In faster scenarios he turns to an **electrician apprenticeship**, knowing it buys only a few years.
He blames owners who keep the gains, and backs **wage support** and **unions**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he couldn't finish a trade in time and Priya's job might wobble.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid adult apprenticeships** and wage support, so retraining doesn't burn their savings.
